claims.text: The proposed framework separately computes lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions using DFT-derived anharmonic phonon scattering, independent electron-phonon coupling calculations, and data-driven corrections.
The framework will predict the total thermal conductivity of pristine, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr within ±10% of experiment from 300 to 1200 K.
The framework will reliably reproduce separate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions below 200 K.
The target material is pristine, defect-free bulk HfNbTaTiZr with no more than trace extrinsic impurities such as oxygen.
DFT-derived atomic-scale lattice structure and electronic band structure determine phonon scattering rates and electron-phonon interaction strengths in HfNbTaTiZr.
Strongly anharmonic phonon interactions are an important thermal-transport mechanism in HfNbTaTiZr.
Modeling anharmonic phonon interactions separately from electronic effects and independently computing electron-phonon coupling prevents conflation of the two heat-transport channels.
Preventing conflation of lattice and electronic transport will reduce prediction errors associated with overlapping transport channels.
Earlier predictive methods modeled thermal transport jointly as a combined effect.
Earlier predictive methods have produced errors exceeding 20%.
Earlier predictive methods fail to capture the proper balance between lattice and electronic heat conduction across the full temperature range.
Low-temperature experiments below 200 K provide observations against which separate lattice and electronic contributions can be validated.
Significant oxygen contamination or other extrinsic defects may make the predictions inapplicable.
The hypothesis may not extend to temperature regimes in which other phenomena, such as magnetic effects, become significant.
Laser-flash analysis can measure the total thermal conductivity needed to test the prediction.
Electrical-conductivity measurements combined with the Wiedemann-Franz law can estimate the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
A measured total thermal conductivity differing from the model prediction by more than ±10% over 300–1200 K would falsify the hypothesis.
Reversed or substantially mismatched predicted and measured low-temperature lattice and electronic trends would falsify the hypothesis.
